headline: New PAC Reported $0 Through Oct. 14, Then $1.2M in Ohio's Senate Race: Half for the Libertarian, Half Against Husted
dek: Buckeye Freedom PAC, registered Oct. 5, names no donors, and its next regular report is due a month after Election Day. On the other side, a group tied by the AP to a MAGA-linked vendor has reported $1.58M backing a socialist and opposing Sherrod Brown.
bottomLine: FEC filings show a super PAC that reported $0 through Oct. 14 then reported $1.2 million backing Ohio's Libertarian Senate candidate and opposing Republican Jon Husted, while another new PAC has reported $1.58 million backing a socialist and opposing Democrat Sherrod Brown. Neither has named a donor. Who is behind them, and whether any of it moves votes, is unknown.

coreFacts.text: Buckeye Freedom PAC reported $1.2 million in independent expenditures in Ohio's U.S. Senate race in a 24-hour report filed Oct. 18, 2026: $600,000 supporting Libertarian William (Bill) Redpath and $600,000 opposing Republican Sen. Jon Husted. Both lines are 'Media Placement and Production' paid to RFO Marketing Partners LLC of Wilmington, Delaware, with a dissemination date of Oct. 17. The report lists the committee's year-to-date total in the race as $1.2 million.

debate.position: Two brand-new PACs with no donors on file have reported $2.8 million in a Senate race, backing third-party candidates and attacking both major-party nominees, and voters deserve to know who paid before anyone assigns blame by party.
debate.argument: Buckeye Freedom PAC registered Oct. 5, showed $0 raised and $0 spent on Oct. 15, then reported $1.2 million in spending three days later, split evenly between backing Libertarian Bill Redpath and attacking Republican Sen. Jon Husted. Its filings name no donor, and its Oct. 18 amendment changed its treasurer, bank and address in one move. That deserves scrutiny, and it hit a Republican. Enough Promises Ohio is the stronger story for the left: its vendor shares a suite with a firm run by Big Dog Strategies, which advises MAGA Inc. But a shared address shows a vendor relationship, not who paid, the donors are undisclosed, and no record shows any coordination with Husted's campaign. Outlets covered the Brown-spoiler story. RockLeak found no coverage of the PAC that spent against a Republican incumbent, and the Fox piece skips both. The fix is the same either way: disclose the donors. Buckeye's next regular report isn't due until Dec. 3, which is too late for an Oct. 17 ad buy.
debate.concedes: The vendor trail from Enough Promises Ohio runs to a firm tied to a MAGA super PAC, Levy says the mailers falsely pose as his campaign, and the spending is aimed at Brown. A reasonable reader can call that an apparent attempt to siphon votes from the Democrat, and I cannot show otherwise because the donors are hidden.

debate.position: Two fresh PACs with no disclosed donors are spending millions to pull votes toward third-party candidates on both sides of a close Ohio race, and the public deserves to know who is paying before Nov. 3.
debate.argument: Enough Promises Ohio registered Sept. 29 and has already reported $1.58 million in spending, yet its only full financial report so far shows $0 raised. Its mail vendor shares a suite with a firm run by Big Dog Strategies, which advises MAGA Inc. and managed Moreno's 2024 win over Brown. Buckeye Freedom PAC registered Oct. 5, reported $0 raised and $0 spent on Oct. 15, then reported $1.2 million in spending three days later. On that same day it changed its address, treasurer and bank, and it names no donor. Levy says the pro-Levy mailers impersonate his campaign and are dirty tricks. The pattern is a lot of money from unknown sources, aimed at third-party candidates and the major-party nominees in a race that polls show is close. That is a transparency failure whatever the intent turns out to be.
debate.concedes: The evidence does not show who funds either group, and a shared address is not proof of who paid. No record shows coordination with Husted's campaign, and no record links the two PACs to each other. Spectrum News notes that both parties have used third-party boosts before. Polls have Levy and Redpath in single digits, so nobody can say this spending changes votes, and Levy's impersonation claim is unverified because RockLeak has not seen the mailers.

debate.position: Two new PACs with no disclosed donors are spending big in Ohio, and until the filings say who is paying, both parties' partisans are guessing about motive.
debate.argument: The filings prove a few things and only those. Buckeye Freedom PAC showed $0 raised and $0 spent on Oct. 15, then reported $1.2 million in spending three days later while moving its address, treasurer and bank. Enough Promises Ohio reported $0 raised through Sept. 30 and has since spent $1.58 million, much of it with a vendor that shares a suite with a firm run by Big Dog Strategies, which advises MAGA Inc. A shared address is a trail, not proof of who paid, and no record links the two PACs to each other or to any campaign. Outlets that call the group GOP-linked are reading a vendor connection as political sponsorship, which is plausible but not shown. The next test comes Oct. 22, when Enough Promises Ohio's pre-general report is due. Buckeye Freedom PAC's next regular report isn't due until Dec. 3, a month after the election.
debate.concedes: The spending against the major-party nominees is roughly matched: $518,609 against Brown and $600,000 against Husted. But the larger and better-documented effort is the pro-Levy money, which hurts Brown, and its vendor trail leads to a firm tied to the Republican side. Critics who read that as a GOP-aligned play have the strongest evidence of anyone so far. Past examples show both parties have used this tactic.

debate.argument: Buckeye Freedom PAC registered Oct. 5, showed $0 raised and $0 spent on Oct. 15, then reported $1.2 million in spending three days later, backing Libertarian Bill Redpath and attacking Sen. Jon Husted. Its filings name no donor, and it changed its address, treasurer and bank on the same day it filed. Enough Promises Ohio shows $0 raised on its only full financial report so far, yet it has reported $1.58 million in spending, mostly backing socialist Greg Levy, and its mail vendor shares a suite with a firm run by Big Dog Strategies, which advises MAGA Inc. Levy himself calls the mailers dirty tricks. Politico's story covered only the Levy PAC, with no mention of Buckeye Freedom PAC or Redpath in the copies RockLeak saw, and RockLeak found no right-leaning outlet covering either group. Voters are being told nothing about who is paying, and Buckeye Freedom PAC's next regular report isn't due until Dec. 3, a month after the Nov. 3 election.

Polls also have Levy and Redpath in single digits, so there is no evidence yet that this spending moves votes.

consensus: All four analysts accept the FEC spending records and agree that neither PAC has disclosed a donor. None treat the shared-vendor link as proof of who funds Enough Promises Ohio, and none claim the polls show the third-party candidates will swing the race.

body: A super PAC that didn't exist until Oct. 5 has reported $1.2 million in ads in Ohio's U.S. Senate race. Half supports Libertarian Bill Redpath. Half opposes Republican Sen. Jon Husted. RockLeak found no news coverage of it.

The group is Buckeye Freedom PAC. Its first two reports, filed Oct. 15, show $0 raised and $0 spent through Oct. 14. On Oct. 18 it reported two $600,000 payments for "media placement and production" to RFO Marketing Partners LLC of Wilmington, Delaware. The filing says the ads first went out Oct. 17.

The same day, it amended its FEC registration. It moved from Hudson, Wisconsin, to a PO box in Columbus, changed treasurers, switched to a bank in McLean, Virginia, and listed a contact email of electgop4usa@gmail.com. Its filings don't name a donor, and RockLeak hasn't seen its ads.

A second new group is working the other side of the race. Enough Promises Ohio registered Sept. 29. From Oct. 5 to Oct. 16 it reported $1.58 million: $1.06 million supporting Greg Levy, an independent socialist candidate, and $519,000 opposing Democrat Sherrod Brown. No record links the two groups.

The AP reported that Enough Promises Ohio's mail vendor uses the same South Carolina office suite as a direct-mail firm run by Big Dog Strategies, which advises President Trump's MAGA Inc. super PAC and ran Republican Bernie Moreno's 2024 win over Brown. A shared address is not proof of who paid, and the AP reported no response from the PAC or Big Dog. Levy has disowned the mailers. He calls them "dirty tricks" that falsely impersonate his campaign. Politico reported that Husted's campaign said it had no involvement with the group.

Why pay for ads backing a long shot? Spectrum News called the pro-Levy mail an apparent attempt to siphon voters from Brown, and noted both parties have done this before. The pro-Redpath ads could work the same way against Husted, but no one behind them has said why they're running.

Third-party candidates are polling in single digits where measured. A co/efficient poll (Oct. 5-6, 925 likely voters, ±3.49 points) had Husted at 44%, Brown 43%, Levy 3% and Redpath 1%. Likely-voter polls with October dates range from Husted ahead by 2 to Brown ahead by 6. Whether any of this spending changes votes is unknown.

Voters may not learn who paid before they vote. Enough Promises Ohio's next report, covering through Oct. 14, is due Oct. 22. Buckeye Freedom PAC already filed that report, showing $0, so its next regular report isn't due until Dec. 3, a month after Election Day.

headline: Elon Musk Gave $158M to the GOP Group Helping Ken Paxton. Polls Still Call It a Coin Flip.
dek: Texans are already voting, and a 2,000-voter poll has Talarico up 48-46, inside the margin of error. Here's where Musk's money went and what's false.
bottomLine: FEC filings confirm that Elon Musk gave $158 million to the Senate GOP's main super PAC in September, and that money went to a new group running ads for Ken Paxton. Polls show James Talarico narrowly ahead, but the leads are inside the margin of error, and Texas polls have underestimated Republicans before. Nobody knows the outcome. The money, the polling and the false rumors spread about the race are all documented.

body: Texans started voting Monday, and the most expensive question in American politics now has a name attached: Elon Musk. FEC filings show Musk wrote two checks to the Senate Leadership Fund in September, $75 million on Sept. 9 and $83 million on Sept. 23. Each time, the Senate GOP's flagship super PAC moved the same amount the next day into Texas PAC, a new affiliate buying ads for Ken Paxton and against James Talarico.

All that money is chasing a race that, by most measures, is a coin flip. A University of Houston Hobby School poll of 2,000 likely voters, taken Oct. 10-14, has Talarico at 48% and Paxton at 46%, inside the ±2.19-point margin of error. Fox News' late-September poll showed a similar 51-49 split. No Democrat has won statewide in Texas since 1994.

Talarico isn't short of money either. His campaign committee reported $60.2 million in third-quarter receipts to the FEC, and the campaign says the total is $64 million counting its joint fundraising arm. He had $14.6 million on hand on Sept. 30, against $4.9 million for Paxton's committee. But outside spending dwarfs both campaigns: AdImpact data cited by the Texas Tribune shows outside groups had spent more than $217 million on ads by the end of September.

Paxton himself sounds uneasy about the help. In audio from a Sept. 24 lobbyist-hosted lunch in Washington, first published by Politico, the attorney general said, "I've never been in a race where I felt less control over the campaign." His campaign says he meant the legal wall between campaigns and super PACs.

The race has also been a test of how fast falsehoods spread. While Talarico was off the trail with the flu, conservative influencers on X spread a claim that he'd been treated at an Ohio mental health facility. The facility denied it, and the AP, Snopes and FactCheck.org all rated it false. Earlier, Paxton's campaign ran an AI-generated ad depicting Talarico reading from a fictional Bible, which FactCheck.org said stripped his real remarks of context and added words he never said.

Then there's the debate that isn't happening. Talarico has accepted several network invitations. As of mid-October, Paxton had accepted none, even after President Trump publicly called for a debate. That puts Texas on track for its first Senate race without a debate in about a quarter century.

Prediction markets lean Talarico. Kalshi traders put his odds at about 62% as of Oct. 20. But Tangle notes that polls underestimated Republicans in Texas in 2024 and 2022, and early voting runs only through Oct. 30. The $158 million question will be answered on Nov. 3.

body: The Senate voted 86-11 to hit Vladimir Putin's economy with sweeping new tariffs and sanctions. On Sept. 18, President Trump signed it. On Friday, Oct. 16, two days before most of its provisions were set to take effect, he signed an executive order setting them aside.

The order invokes the law's own escape hatch, a Section 115 waiver allowed when the president certifies it is "in the national interests of the United States." It waives tariffs of up to 500% on Russian goods, up to 100% secondary tariffs on top buyers of Russian energy, and a long list of new sanctions. It sets no end date: the waivers last until the president or secretary of state decides otherwise. Sanctions imposed under earlier executive orders remain.

The timing points to diesel. On Oct. 9, Trump announced a deal with Putin to move Russian diesel onto world markets, and Treasury issued General License 135 the same day, authorizing Russian diesel transactions through April 2027. NBC reports diesel prices have climbed almost 70% since the Iran war began in February. CBS calculates the U.S. purchase at about 2.2 million barrels, just over half of a single day's U.S. diesel use.

Republicans didn't stay quiet. Sen. Thom Tillis called it "beyond irresponsible." Sen. Ted Cruz said, "I think it was a mistake." Sen. John Cornyn said Graham "would be appalled." Even Sen. Darline Graham, who was appointed to her late brother's seat and is now on the ballot, said she "would choose to keep the pressure on Russia." Democrats including Chuck Schumer and Richard Blumenthal went further, and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called the decision wrong.

The White House says enforcing the sanctions now would "impede ongoing U.S. efforts" to negotiate peace. Trump called it "a very good decision." Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the president wants 60 days to analyze the impact, although the order itself contains no such clock.

Can Congress stop it? Not before the election. Both chambers are in recess until after Nov. 3, and the waiver section requires only a certification and a report, not a vote. Rep. Gregory Meeks has introduced a bill to block the diesel deal, but it can't move until lawmakers return.

Traders aren't betting on a quick payoff for the peace argument. Polymarket puts a Russia-Ukraine ceasefire agreement by Dec. 31 at about 16.5%, and gives roughly 30% odds that Russian diesel actually lands in the U.S. by the end of November.

body: Twenty-two days before the midterms, federal agents showed up at a sitting congresswoman's home. On Oct. 12, Homeland Security Investigations agents searched Rep. Ilhan Omar's Washington home under a warrant the Justice Department says was judicially authorized, as part of "an ongoing federal criminal investigation." Eight days later, there are no charges, and DOJ hasn't publicly said what it suspects.

Reporting from several outlets, citing people familiar with the probe, points to immigration paperwork. Investigators are reportedly looking at whether Omar's late father lied or left information off his forms, and whether Omar was 17 or 18 when he became a citizen in 2000. Omar says she became a citizen before she turned 18. Grand jury subpoenas went to relatives, including, per The New York Times, her sister Sahra Noor. Agents took Omar's cellphone, and The Washington Post reported they took her passport too.

The search itself is now in dispute. In an Oct. 16 letter, Omar's lawyers say agents ignored a magistrate judge's instructions meant to protect her rights as a member of Congress: notify the House General Counsel and hand her the warrant at the start. DOJ says the letter is "riddled with false allegations and inaccuracies" and that it followed every court order.

Administration officials haven't been shy. Border czar Tom Homan told Fox News on Oct. 18 that denaturalization "could happen" "if the evidence points that way," and that he'd been told investigators have "a strong case," while saying he didn't know the specifics. DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin has repeated the claim that Omar married her brother, which Snopes rates unfounded and for which no public evidence exists.

Trump said the search had nothing to do with him and deferred to DOJ, but days earlier he told a Tennessee rally that "JD Vance and our people are looking at it very strongly." House Democratic leaders called the search "corrupt weaponization." NBC notes DOJ has no blanket 60-day pre-election blackout, but its policy says investigative steps shouldn't be timed to affect an election.

Some of this has come up before. A 2019 inquiry into Omar's immigration history found insufficient evidence for a full investigation, The Washington Post reported. A 2019 request by her staff to change her listed birth year with the Minnesota Legislative Reference Library is documented, but even Fox News notes it "does not establish that Omar falsified immigration records."
Traders are skeptical of a fast case. Polymarket puts federal charges by Oct. 31 at about 6.5% and by Dec. 31 at about 22.5%. Omar's Minneapolis seat isn't considered at risk on Nov. 3.
